in area rivers and streams, and poor drainage ponding on roadways 
has already occurred. As drier and colder air flows into the region 
tonight, temperatures are expected to drop dramatically into the 
upper 20s to lower 40s by early Thursday morning. This, paired with 
north-northwesterly breezes gusting 15-30 mph due to a low level jet 
on the back end of our rain system, will make for apparent 
temperatures in the mid 20s to mid 30s when it's time to head to 
school or work. This will be some of the chilliest air we've had in 
a while. Thursday during the day, high pressure should decrease 
winds, but temperatures will still be slightly below average for 
this time of year with widespread highs in the 50s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Another frontal system is headed for our forecast area 
Thursday night through Friday night. Model agreement is exceptional 
for a large swath of rain to overspread the region late Thursday 
night and early Friday morning out ahead of a strengthening low 
pressure system. A vigorous shortwave will dig over the western 
Great Lakes, merging with a frontal system over the Midwest to help 
intensify low pressure to our west. This storm will rapidly move 
northeastward, passing near or right over our region (most likely 
along the St. Lawrence Valley) Friday afternoon and crossing into 
northern Maine Friday evening. Precipitation may be impacted by some 
our topography. A strong southwesterly low level jet will produce 
downsloping in the northern Champlain Valley, while our western 
slopes have a little bit of a boost in rainfall amounts. The near 
surface winds will also likely be strong out of the south on Friday, 
though rain could limit mixing. Any breaks in precipitation should 
support 20-30 MPH localized gusts, higher on summits closer to a 
strong low level jet. Lake Champlain should also see higher gusts in 
southerly channeling.

A cold front will sweep through the area Friday night, sharply 
lowering temperatures 10 to 15 degrees from Friday evening to 
Saturday morning. Temperatures will likely dip below freezing for 
most if not all locations across the area with only those near Lake 
Champlain and immediately near the St. Lawrence River staying just 
above freezing. As temperatures fall, snow levels will also drop, 
falling to 500-1000ft agl by Saturday. It will be a race against dry 
air for the temperatures fall at the same time the atmosphere dries 
out. If there is some overlap in saturated air and cold air Friday 
night or Saturday morning, we're more likely to see some snowflakes 
or rain/snow mix in the Champlain Valley. Snow looks highly likely 
in the higher terrain with temperatures in the 20s. Snowfall impacts 
will be minimal with road and ground temperatures well above 
freezing, and with only marginal surface temperatures outside of the 
highest elevations, snow will likely be of a wet character, with 
minor accumulation only on the highest elevations and mainly on 
vegetation only. In addition to the precipitation Friday night into 
Saturday, winds will turn to the northwest with better confidence in 
stronger winds Saturday due to a lack of precipitation limitations 
that existed during the day Friday. With an influx of cold northwest 
air, lapse rates will quickly steepen with strong mixing late Friday 
night and early Saturday morning. Highest wind gusts will be 
widespread 30-40 mph with gusts above 40-45 mph on summits, 
potentially as high as 45-60 mph. While we don't anticipate needing 
a Wind Advisory (for gusts greater than 46 mph), trends will need to 
be watched closely going forward.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Ridging will start to build over the region for the 
latter half of the weekend, keeping us under northwest flow. Can't 
rule out a few stray showers over the higher terrain early Sunday, 
but overall expect a dry though chilly second half of the weekend. 
The dry weather will persist through mid week as high pressure keeps 
hold over the Northeast CONUS. Temperatures will warm through the 
period, with highs to be in the upper 50s/low 60s by Tuesday.
